To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
TLR9 activated B cells can be induced to produce IL-10, and that IL-10 producing B cells have the capacity to inhibit T cell proliferation and cytokine production.

TLR signaling in B cells during HIV pathogenesis is associated with both antibody-dependent effector functions and TLR-driven B cell regulatory functions, including the induction of IL-10 producing regulatory B cells (Bregs).
TLR9 activated B cells have regulatory effects on HIV-specific CD4 T cells and TLR9 activation of B cells is associated with reduced HIV viral load in patients on antiretroviral therapy (ART).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of TLR signaling in the generation of HIV driven chronic inflammation, the effector functions of TLR activated B cells, and the regulatory functions of TLR stimulated B cells.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
B cell effector and regulatory function is context-dependent and that both effector and regulatory roles for B cells in HIV pathogenesis are likely to occur.
B cells can exert both effector and regulatory roles during HIV infection.
B cells have a dual role in HIV pathogenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
B cells are important in the control of HIV infection.
HIV infection leads to a dysregulation of B cell functions, which is likely to be driven by TLR activation.
B cells are not just a passive target in chronic immune activation but rather an active player in the pathogenesis of HIV disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the role of B cells is not limited to antibody production.
B cells are not only involved in HIV pathogenesis through antibody production, but that B cells also exert effector functions through cytokine production.
B cells may play a regulatory role in the control of HIV replication.
